spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Coined by Jeffrey Palermo in 2008, **Onion Architecture** places the **Domain Model** (entities, value objects, aggregates, domain events with zero ORM/HTTP annotations) at the center, surrounded by **Domain Services**.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Onion Architecture Inward Dependency Rule (UI/Web -> AppSvc -> DomSvc -> Infra -> Domain); PlaceOrder Execution Through Ports & Adapters (OrderController -> PlaceOrderUC -> Order Domain -> PostgresAdapter).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Onion, Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters), and Clean Architecture share the exact same Dependency Inversion core, differing mainly in ring naming. Explore how Onion Architecture pairs with Hexagonal Architecture, Domain-Driven Design, and Transactional Outbox.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore how Onion Architecture pairs with Hexagonal Architecture, Domain-Driven Design, and Transactional Outbox.

learningJourney.title: What is Onion Architecture

explanation.foundation: Coined by Jeffrey Palermo in 2008, **Onion Architecture** places the **Domain Model** (entities, value objects, aggregates, domain events with zero ORM/HTTP annotations) at the center, surrounded by **Domain Services**, **Application Services** (use cases + output port interfaces like `OrderRepository` and `PaymentGateway`), and finally the outermost **Infrastructure & UI** ring (JPA, jOOQ, FastAPI, Kafka adapters).
explanation.core: The **Dependency Rule** is absolute: source-code imports may only point inward toward the center; inner rings never import outer-ring frameworks.
explanation.deepDive: In production deployments of Onion Architecture, watch how what is onion architecture interacts with tail latency, retry amplification, and partial failures. An architectural style that places domain entities and business rules at the center, forcing all dependencies—frameworks, databases, and UI—to point strictly inward through interfaces.

sectionDiagram.title: Onion Architecture Inward Dependency Rule
sectionDiagram.summary: Outer adapters implement interfaces defined in inner rings; the Domain Model imports only the language standard library.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Onion Architecture (and why N-tier couples to SQL)

explanation.foundation: In classic N-tier architectures, the database sits at the bottom of the dependency graph: business services import ORM entities and SQL clients directly.
explanation.core: Upgrading Hibernate, swapping PostgreSQL for DynamoDB, or testing complex pricing rules forces you to boot a 6-second Spring context or mock SQL cursors.
explanation.deepDive: Inverting dependencies lets pure domain logic compile and run thousands of tests in under 15 ms with zero I/O.

ideas.title: Rich Domain Models Over Anemic Bags
ideas.description: Push invariant checks (`order.confirm()`, `wallet.debit(amount)`) onto domain aggregates instead of leaving entities as getter/setter DTOs with duplicated service validation.

ideas.title: CQRS Bypass for Complex Reads
ideas.description: Keep Onion aggregates for command/write paths, and allow slim read-only query projections that map SQL rows straight to response DTOs without N+1 aggregate loading.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Onion Architecture without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: If latency budgets leave no room for synchronous retries, isolate your core business logic from Spring, SQLAlchemy, or Kafka by defining repository and gateway interfaces inside the domain/application ring and implementing them in the outermost infrastructure ring.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

decisionExercise.prompt: When Onion Architecture experiences a sudden 5x traffic spike alongside a slow downstream dependency, which engineering choice best protects system stability?

options.label: Increase retry counts and remove client timeouts so every request eventually succeeds.
options.explanation: Unbounded retries multiply load on an already struggling dependency and exhaust worker pools.

options.label: Enforce strict latency budgets, bounded jittered retries, and graceful fallback or load shedding.
options.explanation: Bounding retries and isolating slow paths preserves healthy capacity and keeps tail latency predictable.

learningJourney.title: Where Onion Architecture shines (and where it is overkill)

explanation.foundation: Think of **Where Onion Architecture shines (and where it is overkill)** as the intuition layer for Onion Architecture: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.
explanation.core: Apply Onion Architecture to long-lived, invariant-heavy domains; skip the mapping overhead for simple CRUD or analytics pipelines.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, where onion architecture shines (and where it is overkill) becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. An architectural style that places domain entities and business rules at the center, forcing all dependencies—frameworks, databases, and UI—to point strictly inward through interfaces.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Billing Ledgers, Underwriting & Fulfillment
benefits: Protects complex state machines and regulatory rules from framework upgrades and vendor swaps (e.g., Stripe to Adyen).
costs: Adds explicit mappers between domain aggregates, JPA/ORM entities, and API DTOs (15–25% more files).

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Fast In-Memory Domain Unit Testing
benefits: In-memory repository fakes verify 80%+ of business rules in milliseconds without Docker/Testcontainers.
costs: Still requires contract/integration tests against real DBs to catch SQL unique-index and lock semantics.

comparison.choice: Avoid: Simple CRUD Services & dbt/Spark Pipelines
benefits: Direct table-to-JSON handlers or set-based SQL jobs ship faster without multi-ring mapping boilerplate.
costs: Forcing 4 rings onto a 2-endpoint CRUD service slows iteration for zero architectural benefit.

learningJourney.title: How Ring Boundaries are enforced in CI

explanation.foundation: Think of **How Ring Boundaries are enforced in CI** as the intuition layer for Onion Architecture: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.
explanation.core: Under deadline pressure, developers accidentally import `infra.postgres` or `@Entity` annotations into `domain/`. Prevent architectural drift automatically in CI using **ArchUnit** (Java/Kotlin) or **`import-linter`** (Python) so violating imports fail the build immediately.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, how ring boundaries are enforced in ci becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. An architectural style that places domain entities and business rules at the center, forcing all dependencies—frameworks, databases, and UI—to point strictly inward through interfaces.

learningJourney.markdownContent:
```java
// ArchUnit CI rule enforcing Onion Architecture ring boundaries
Architectures.onionArchitecture()
  .domainModels("com.acme.orders.domain.model..")
  .domainServices("com.acme.orders.domain.service..")
  .applicationServices("com.acme.orders.application..")
  .adapter("persistence", "com.acme.orders.infra.postgres..")
  .adapter("rest", "com.acme.orders.infra.web..");
```

_recommendedProblem.prompt: Design a distributed rate limiter at the API gateway handling 500,000 req/sec across 10+ stateless API nodes, 10M active identity-policy pairs (~2 GB primary state), enforcing per-user and per-IP quotas across second/minute/hour windows within <= 2 ms p99 overhead and graceful Redis failover.
